content: The recommended dosing for acai palm (Euterpe oleracea), commonly known as acai, varies depending on the indication. While there is no standard dosage, acai is often consumed as a food. For therapeutic purposes, anthocyanin or flavonoid supplementation derived from acai berries is typically dosed between 200 mg and 1500 mg per day. Acai berry juice can be consumed as needed, provided it is well-tolerated. Acai berry extract is commonly taken at a dose of 500 mg daily. Acai is traditionally used for its adaptogenic properties, helping the body adapt to internal and external stressors, combat fatigue, and enhance stamina. It has also been used for anti-aging purposes and to support heart health, bone and joint health, prostate and urinary tract health, and to manage hypercholesterolemia. Additionally, it is believed to aid in cleansing the body and reducing inflammation. Reported adverse effects include diarrhea, fever, and skin ulcers. Acai is recognized as a potent antioxidant with a high oxygen radical absorbance capacity (ORAC) value, which supports the body’s natural defenses against free radical damage, infections, and diseases. It may help maintain healthy HDL cholesterol levels, improve blood circulation, and reduce the risk of arteriosclerosis, stroke, and heart attack. Acai also exhibits COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitory activity, which may contribute to its anti-inflammatory effects. Furthermore, it may act as a vasodilator, potentially benefiting individuals with cardiovascular disease, and it has been suggested as a possible aid in managing lupus. Regarding pregnancy and lactation, there is no specific category assigned to acai. However, it is generally considered acceptable, as controlled studies in pregnant women have not demonstrated any evidence of fetal risk.
